title: The Untold Story of Abishai Trying to Kill Saul While David Held Him Back
paragraphs:
The Untold Story of Abishai Trying to Kill Saul While David Held Him Back
The Night Two Men Entered the Darkness… And Only One Understood the Heart of God
There are moments in Scripture that feel too human to be fake.

Moments where rage trembles under the skin. Moments where revenge feels justified. Moments where loyalty collides with restraint. Moments where one decision can either crown a man… or corrupt him forever.
Deep in the wilderness of Ziph, under a sky heavy with silence and war, two men slipped through enemy lines while thousands slept.
One carried a spear. The other carried a promise.
One wanted blood. The other feared God.
And history almost changed forever.
Most people remember David sparing Saul. Few remember the fire burning inside Abishai.
But if you look closely at this story, you may discover something terrifying about yourself.
Because most believers are far more like Abishai than they realize.
And most of us have secretly wished God would finally let us strike back.
The story unfolds in 1 Samuel 26.
Saul was still hunting David like an animal. Even after David had already spared Saul once in the cave at En Gedi. Even after David proved his innocence. Even after David chose mercy over vengeance.
Saul returned to chasing him anyway.
That alone already reveals one of the hardest truths in spiritual life:
Not everyone changes after receiving mercy.
Some people survive your kindness and continue trying to destroy you.
Saul gathered three thousand chosen men from Israel and marched again into the wilderness searching for David.
David learned where Saul camped. And then something shocking happened.
David volunteered to walk directly into the camp at night.
Not around it. Not near it. Into it.
Scripture says:
“אָז אָמַר דָּוִד אֶל־אֲחִימֶלֶךְ הַחִתִּי וְאֶל־אֲבִישַׁי בֶּן־צְרוּיָה אֲחִי יוֹאָב לֵאמֹר מִי־יֵרֵד אִתִּי אֶל־שָׁאוּל אֶל־הַמַּחֲנֶה”
Transliteration:
“Mi-yered itti el-Sha’ul el-hamachaneh?”
Translation:
“Who will go down with me to Saul in the camp?”
— 1 Samuel 26:6
The Hebrew phrase “mi-yered itti” literally carries the sense of descending into danger together. Not merely accompanying. Descending. Entering darkness willingly.
Abishai answered immediately.
“I will go down with you.”
Of course he would.
Abishai was a warrior. A fierce protector. The son of Zeruiah. Brother of Joab. A man known for violence, loyalty, and battlefield intensity.
He loved David. But he also hated David’s enemies.
And sometimes those two emotions become dangerously tangled.
That night, God caused a supernatural sleep to fall over Saul’s camp.
Scripture says:
“כִּי תַּרְדֵּמַת יְהוָה נָפְלָה עֲלֵיהֶם”
Transliteration:
“Ki tardemat YHWH nafelah aleihem.”
Translation:
“For a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen upon them.”
— 1 Samuel 26:12

The phrase “tardemat YHWH” is extraordinary. This was not ordinary exhaustion. This was divine intervention. The same kind of supernatural sleep mentioned elsewhere in Scripture when God moves powerfully.
God Himself created the opening.
And suddenly there it was.
Saul asleep. The spear beside his head. The king vulnerable. Defenseless. Exposed.
The man who destroyed David’s peace. The man who hunted him relentlessly. The man who turned armies against him. The man who drove him into caves. The man who weaponized jealousy.
Right there.
Breathing.
One strike away from ending everything.
And then Abishai whispered words that probably sounded perfectly reasonable.
“God has delivered your enemy into your hand today.”
In Hebrew:
“סִגַּר אֱלֹהִים הַיּוֹם אֶת־אוֹיִבְךָ בְּיָדֶךָ”
Transliteration:
“Siggar Elohim hayom et oyivekha beyadekha.”
Translation:
“God has delivered your enemy into your hand today.”
— 1 Samuel 26:8
Notice the language carefully.
Abishai interpreted opportunity as permission.
That mistake still destroys believers today.
Just because the door opened does not mean God told you to walk through it.
Just because revenge became possible does not mean revenge became righteous.
Just because someone finally became vulnerable does not mean heaven authorized your retaliation.
Abishai continued:
“Now therefore, please, let me strike him at once with the spear, right to the earth; and I will not have to strike him twice.”
That final line is chilling.
“I will not have to strike him twice.”
Abishai was confident. Efficient. Experienced.
This was not emotional chaos. This was calculated execution.
And if we are honest, there are moments where many of us understand him.
The betrayal. The humiliation. The lies. The injustice. The years stolen. The wounds left behind.
Some people have hurt us so deeply that mercy feels offensive.
We tell ourselves:
“They deserve it.” “God is giving me my chance.” “This is justice.”
But vengeance can disguise itself as discernment.
And wounded people often call their anger ‘wisdom.’
Then David said something that separates true spiritual authority from flesh-driven power.
“Do not destroy him.”
In Hebrew:
“אַל־תַּשְׁחִיתֵהוּ”
Transliteration:
“Al-tashchitehu.”
Translation:
“Do not destroy him.”
— 1 Samuel 26:9
David continued:
“Who can stretch out his hand against the LORD’s anointed and remain guiltless?”
The Hebrew phrase is:
“בִּמְשִׁיחַ יְהוָה”
“Bimshiach YHWH.”
“The LORD’s anointed.”
This is where modern readers often struggle.
Because Saul was corrupt. Emotionally unstable. Violent. Jealous. Disobedient.
Yet David still recognized that Saul’s position had once been established by God.
David understood something terrifying:
If he gained the throne through sinful revenge, the throne itself would poison him.
David refused to build a God-given future through flesh-driven methods.
That is a word many believers desperately need.
You cannot establish a holy future through unholy behavior.
Not in ministry. Not in relationships. Not in leadership. Not online. Not behind closed doors.
The method matters.
Character matters.
Hidden obedience matters.
David would rather remain hunted than become corrupted.
Read that again slowly.
David would rather suffer longer than sin sooner.
That is spiritual maturity.
Most people want God’s promises. Few people want God’s process.
Abishai saw an obstacle. David saw a test.
Abishai saw an enemy. David saw accountability before God.
Abishai thought killing Saul would end the problem. David understood killing Saul could create a far worse problem inside his own soul.
Then David says something deeply prophetic:
“As the LORD lives, the LORD shall strike him, or his day shall come to die, or he shall go out to battle and perish.”
— 1 Samuel 26:10
David trusted God with timing.
That is one of the hardest forms of faith.
Not believing God exists. Not believing God speaks.
Believing God can handle your enemies without your sinful interference.
Sometimes restraint is harder than warfare.
Sometimes obedience feels weaker than retaliation.
Sometimes holiness looks passive to angry people.
But heaven measures strength differently.
The world celebrates people who clap back. Heaven honors people who remain surrendered.
And perhaps the most painful part of this story is this:
Abishai genuinely thought he was helping.
He was loyal. Protective. Passionate.
But passion without discernment can become destruction.
Many believers today accidentally become Abishai.
They defend truth without love. Correct people without mercy. Attack others while claiming righteousness. Use spiritual language to justify fleshly behavior.
Not every battle that can be fought should be fought.
Not every enemy needs your spear.
Not every opportunity for revenge came from God.
David took Saul’s spear and water jug instead.
Why the spear?

Because the spear represented Saul’s authority. Throughout Saul’s life, the spear symbolized his violence, power, paranoia, and control. Saul repeatedly tried to pin David to the wall with that spear.
Now David held it.
But he refused to become Saul while defeating Saul.
That line alone could break a person open.
Many people become the very thing that wounded them.
The abused become abusive. The rejected become rejecting. The betrayed become betrayers. The manipulated become manipulators.
Pain reproduces itself unless surrendered to God.
David interrupted that cycle.
And perhaps that is the hidden miracle of this story.
Not merely that Saul survived.
But that David’s heart survived.
Because power changes people. Especially wounded people.
And there are moments when the greatest victory is not defeating your enemy.
It is refusing to become them.
The Greek translation found in the Septuagint preserves the gravity beautifully.
David says:
“Μὴ ταπεινώσῃς αὐτόν.”
“Do not humble him down violently.”
The ancient language preserves restraint. Restraint is not weakness. Restraint is governed strength.
Even Jesus later echoed this deeper kingdom principle.
In the Garden of Gethsemane, when Peter drew a sword to defend Christ, Jesus stopped him.
Violence has a seductive logic.
Especially when protecting someone you love.
Peter and Abishai actually mirror each other.
Both believed they were defending God’s chosen king. Both reached for violence. Both misunderstood the kingdom.
And both were corrected.
Jesus said:
“Put your sword back into its place.”
— Matthew 26:52
David had already lived that principle generations earlier.
The kingdom of God is not advanced through uncontrolled vengeance.
This story also exposes another uncomfortable truth.
Some of us secretly want permission to hate people who hurt us.
We pray for justice, but deep down we crave retaliation.
We say:
“God fight for me.”
But internally we mean:
“God let me watch.”
Yet David trusted God enough to release the outcome.
That does not mean Saul’s behavior was acceptable. It was evil.
Mercy is not denial. Forgiveness is not pretending abuse never happened.
David still fled. Still protected himself. Still recognized danger.
Biblical mercy is not enabling evil.
It is refusing to let evil reshape your soul.
Somebody reading this has been carrying a spear emotionally for years.
A conversation you replay. A betrayal you cannot release. A wound you rehearse every night. A person you still mentally punish.
And maybe God brought you to this story because your heart has been standing over sleeping Saul for far too long.
You have the spear in your hand.
The opportunity. The evidence. The rage. The perfect moment.
And heaven whispers:
“Do not destroy him.”
Not because God ignores justice. But because God cares about what hatred is slowly turning you into.
Some revenge destroys the target. Other revenge destroys the person holding the spear.
David walked away carrying only the spear and the water jug.
The water jug matters too.
Water represents life. Sustenance. Preservation.
David spared both Saul’s authority and Saul’s life.
And then from a distance, David called out to Saul.
Not as an assassin. But as a grieving servant.
That emotional tension is what makes this story unforgettable.
David loved someone who became dangerous.
Many people understand that pain.
A parent. A spouse. A friend. A leader. A mentor.
Someone once safe became unsafe.
And one of the deepest griefs in human existence is mourning people who are still alive.
David knew Saul was broken. But David refused to answer brokenness with greater brokenness.
That restraint eventually prepared David for kingship.
Because the throne was never the true test.
The cave was. The wilderness was. The hidden nights were.
Who you become while waiting on God matters more than the thing you are waiting for.
And maybe that is why this story still convicts hearts thousands of years later.
Because every person eventually faces a moment where they must decide:
Will pain turn me into Saul? Will rage turn me into Abishai? Or will surrender transform me into someone who trusts God like David?
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
And if you know someone battling anger, betrayal, church hurt, rejection, family wounds, or secret bitterness, send this to them tonight.
Some people do not need another argument. They need their soul interrupted.
The most dangerous revenge is the kind that slowly makes you resemble the person who wounded you.
